notes:
Task and constraints: Sort values by increasing frequency; ties are ordered by decreasing numeric value.
Idea: Count each value's frequency and sort by the key `(frequency, -value)`, so rarer values come first and larger values precede smaller values on frequency ties.
Technique and why it applies: The two-part sort key encodes increasing frequency followed by decreasing value for ties.
Invariant: The comparator orders every value first by occurrence count and then by descending numeric value.
Edge cases: Negative values and duplicates are handled; all copies of one value share the same frequency and sort key.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The two-part sort key encodes increasing frequency followed by decreasing value for ties.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true when concatenating each word array produces the same string.
Idea: Concatenate all words in each array and compare the resulting strings.
Technique and why it applies: Joining both word arrays removes irrelevant element boundaries before equality comparison.
Invariant: The joined string represents the full character sequence regardless of how characters are split among array elements.
Edge cases: Different word boundaries do not matter; empty arrays or empty strings are valid and can concatenate to the empty string.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(total characters) space for joined strings.
complexity_reason: Joining both word arrays removes irrelevant element boundaries before equality comparison.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest sum among all customer account rows.
Idea: Sum each customer's account row and track the maximum row total.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing row totals directly identifies the customer with the greatest combined account wealth.
Invariant: The current maximum is the greatest wealth among all rows processed so far.
Edge cases: Each row may contain multiple accounts; nonnegative balances allow initialization at zero; at least one customer is guaranteed.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Comparing row totals directly identifies the customer with the greatest combined account wealth.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decode G, (), and (al) as G, o, and al respectively.
Idea: Replace each encoded token `(al)` with `al` and each `()` with `o`, leaving literal `G` unchanged.
Technique and why it applies: The two token replacements implement the parser's complete set of encodings.
Invariant: The output string is the decoded command sequence after all supported tokens have been replaced.
Edge cases: The token patterns are well-formed and non-overlapping; replacement order handles the longer `(al)` token before `()`.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: The two token replacements implement the parser's complete set of encodings.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count words containing only characters present in allowed.
Idea: Build a set of allowed characters and count each word whose every character belongs to that set.
Technique and why it applies: Set membership checks every character against the permitted alphabet and rejects a word at its first forbidden character.
Invariant: A word is counted only if the scan finds no character outside the allowed set.
Edge cases: An empty word is consistent; repeated letters are allowed as long as each letter is allowed.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(alphabet size) space.
complexity_reason: Set membership checks every character against the permitted alphabet and rejects a word at its first forbidden character.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of matches needed to determine a winner among n teams.
Idea: Return `n-1`, since each match eliminates exactly one team and the tournament ends with one winner.
Technique and why it applies: Every match removes one of the original n teams from contention, leaving exactly n-1 eliminations.
Invariant: The number of remaining teams decreases by one per match until it reaches one.
Edge cases: For n=1, no match is needed; n is positive.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Every match removes one of the original n teams from contention, leaving exactly n-1 eliminations.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true when the first and second halves contain the same number of vowels.
Idea: Count case-insensitive vowels in the first half and second half, then compare the two counts.
Technique and why it applies: Counting vowels separately in equal halves directly tests whether their vowel totals match.
Invariant: The two counters represent the vowel totals of the corresponding equal-length halves.
Edge cases: Uppercase and lowercase vowels both count; the input length is even under the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Counting vowels separately in equal halves directly tests whether their vowel totals match.

notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize units loaded while respecting the truck's box capacity.
Idea: Sort box types by units per box descending, greedily take as many as fit from each type, and stop when truck capacity reaches zero.
Technique and why it applies: Taking boxes with the highest units per box first is optimal under a single total capacity constraint.
Invariant: At each step, the chosen boxes have the greatest available unit density, maximizing units for the remaining capacity.
Edge cases: A type may contribute only some of its boxes; zero remaining capacity ends the loop; no more boxes than available are taken.
Complexity: O(k log k) time and O(1) auxiliary space aside from sorting.
complexity_reason: Taking boxes with the highest units per box first is optimal under a single total capacity constraint.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given encoded[i]=arr[i] XOR arr[i+1] and arr[0], reconstruct arr.
Idea: Start the output with `first` and recover each next value as `out[i] XOR encoded[i]`.
Technique and why it applies: The self-inverse property of XOR reconstructs the next array value from the previous value and its encoding.
Invariant: Because XORing the encoded pair with the known prior value cancels that prior value, each next element is recovered exactly.
Edge cases: An empty encoded array returns `[first]`; output length is encoded length plus one.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: The self-inverse property of XOR reconstructs the next array value from the previous value and its encoding.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum altitude reached from initial altitude zero.
Idea: Maintain current altitude as a prefix sum of `gain` and update the best altitude after each step, initialized to zero.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix sums model altitude after each segment, and retaining zero accounts for the starting point.
Invariant: `cur` is the altitude after the processed gains and `best` is the maximum altitude reached including the starting point.
Edge cases: All gains may be negative; initial altitude zero remains a candidate maximum; empty gains return zero.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Prefix sums model altitude after each segment, and retaining zero accounts for the starting point.
